def: Polymers are large molecules (macromolecules) made of many repeating small units called monomers joined by covalent bonds.
points: Based on source: natural (cellulose, rubber), semi-synthetic (cellulose acetate), synthetic (polythene, nylon).
Based on structure: linear (PVC), branched (glycogen), cross-linked or network (bakelite).
Based on mode of polymerisation: addition polymers (formed by addition of monomers, no loss of atoms) and condensation polymers (formed with loss of a small molecule like water).

Based on molecular forces: elastomers (rubber-like, weak forces), fibres (strong forces, e.g. nylon), thermoplastics (soften on heating, e.g. polythene), thermosetting (hard permanently, e.g. bakelite).
Monomers are the repeating small units from which the polymer chain is built.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Polymers"] --> B["By source natural synthetic"]
  A --> C["By structure linear branched cross linked"]
  A --> D["By polymerisation addition condensation"]
  A --> E["By forces elastomer fibre thermoplastic thermoset"]

example: Polythene is a synthetic, linear, addition, thermoplastic polymer made from ethene monomers.
tip: Give all four classification bases with one example each for a complete 5-mark answer.

def: Addition polymerisation is the process in which monomer molecules with multiple bonds add to one another repeatedly without loss of any atom, to form a polymer.
points: Occurs mainly with monomers having a carbon-carbon double bond (alkenes) or similar unsaturation.
Proceeds by a chain reaction mechanism: initiation, propagation and termination.
An initiator (free radical, cation or anion) starts the reaction by opening the double bond.
The double bond breaks and each monomer adds to the growing chain, repeating many times.
No small molecule is lost; the polymer has the same empirical composition as the monomer.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Initiator starts reaction"] --> B["Double bond opens"]
  B --> C["Monomer adds to chain"]
  C --> D["Chain grows by repetition"]
  D --> E["Termination gives polymer"]

example: Polymerisation of propene (CH2=CH-CH3) gives polypropylene, used for ropes and containers.
tip: Name the three mechanism steps (initiation, propagation, termination) - examiners specifically check for these terms.

def: Condensation polymerisation is the process in which monomers having two or more reactive functional groups combine repeatedly, with the loss of small molecules like water or alcohol, to form a polymer.
points: Monomers usually have two different functional groups (bifunctional), such as a diacid and a diamine, or a diacid and a diol.
A small molecule (commonly water) is eliminated at each linking step.
The polymer chain grows by repeated condensation reactions between monomer units.
Resulting polymer often has ester (-COO-) or amide (-CONH-) linkages.
Examples: nylon-6,6 (polyamide, from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid) and terylene/PET (polyester, from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Diacid monomer"] --> C["Condensation reaction"]
  B["Diamine or diol monomer"] --> C
  C --> D["Polymer chain with amide or ester links"]
  C --> E["Small molecule water released"]

example: Nylon-6,6 is made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, releasing water at each amide bond formed.
tip: Clearly mention 'loss of small molecule such as water' - this is the key difference from addition polymerisation, often asked to distinguish the two.

def: Copolymerisation is a type of addition polymerisation in which two or more different monomers combine together to form a polymer called a copolymer.
points: Unlike a homopolymer (one type of monomer), a copolymer is built from two or more different monomers.
The arrangement of monomer units in the chain can be random, alternating, block, or graft.
Copolymers often combine useful properties of both monomers, e.g. strength and flexibility.
Buna-S is a copolymer of 1,3-butadiene and styrene, used to make synthetic rubber (tyres).
Buna-N is a copolymer of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile, oil-resistant rubber.
formula: n (monomer A) + m (monomer B) -> copolymer chain of A and B units

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Monomer A butadiene"] --> C["Copolymerisation"]
  B["Monomer B styrene"] --> C
  C --> D["Copolymer Buna S rubber"]

example: Buna-S rubber (butadiene + styrene) is used for making vehicle tyres due to its toughness and abrasion resistance.
tip: Name at least two copolymer examples with their monomers (Buna-S, Buna-N) - commonly asked in 2-mark questions.

def: Natural rubber is a natural polymer of isoprene (cis-1,4-polyisoprene) obtained from the latex of rubber trees; synthetic rubbers are man-made elastomers prepared by polymerisation of suitable monomers.
points: Natural rubber is a 1,4-addition polymer of isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) with cis configuration, giving it elasticity.
Raw natural rubber is soft and sticky; it is strengthened by vulcanisation.
Vulcanisation: heating raw rubber with sulphur, which forms cross-links (sulphur bridges) between polymer chains, increasing strength, elasticity and reducing stickiness.
Synthetic rubbers (elastomers) are made by polymerising dienes, e.g. neoprene (from chloroprene), Buna-S, Buna-N.
Synthetic rubbers often have better resistance to oil, heat or chemicals than natural rubber.
formula: Vulcanisation: rubber + sulphur --(heat)--> cross linked rubber (sulphur bridges)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Raw natural rubber soft sticky"] --> B["Heated with sulphur"]
  B --> C["Sulphur cross links form between chains"]
  C --> D["Vulcanised rubber strong elastic"]

example: Vulcanised rubber is used to make automobile tyres, which need both strength and elasticity.
tip: Mention the role of sulphur cross-links clearly - this is the exact mechanism examiners expect in the vulcanisation answer.

def: Biodegradable polymers are polymers that can be broken down into simple, non-toxic substances by the action of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi) in the environment.
points: Unlike conventional plastics (polythene, PVC) which persist for years, biodegradable polymers decompose naturally, reducing pollution.
They usually contain ester or amide linkages that microorganisms can hydrolyse easily.
PHBV (poly beta-hydroxybutyrate-co-beta-hydroxyvalerate) is a biodegradable copolyester used in packaging and medical sutures.
Nylon-2-nylon-6 is a biodegradable polyamide copolymer made from glycine and amino caproic acid.
Biodegradable polymers are important for reducing plastic waste and environmental pollution.
formula: No single formula - key feature: ester/amide linkages broken down by microorganisms

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Biodegradable polymer"] --> B["Buried in soil or disposed"]
  B --> C["Microorganisms act on it"]
  C --> D["Hydrolysis of ester or amide links"]
  D --> E["Simple non toxic products"]

example: PHBV is used to make biodegradable packaging material and dissolvable surgical sutures.
tip: Give one example (PHBV or Nylon-2-nylon-6) with its use, and link the answer to 'reducing environmental pollution'.
